keyVerseText: And Zorobabel begat Abiud; and Abiud begat Eliakim; and Eliakim begat Azor;
rootMeaning: The name Ἐλιακείμ (Eliakeím) originates from the Hebrew אֶלְיָקִים (ʼElyâqîym), which means "God raises" or "God sets up." This root meaning conveys the idea of God actively elevating or establishing someone, suggesting divine empowerment or appointment. Such a name reflects a theological affirmation that God is the ultimate source of authority and position, beyond mere human designation.
usageInScripture: The word Ἐλιακείμ appears three times in Scripture, consistently translated as "Eliakim" or in the phrase "which was the son of Eliakim." This consistency indicates that the term primarily functions as a proper noun identifying specific individuals, including an ancestor of Jesus. The usage highlights the name's role in genealogical records, emphasizing the continuity of God's providential plan through Israelite lineage.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Ἐλιακείμ as "God raises" enriches our appreciation of biblical genealogy by reminding us that the leaders and ancestors mentioned are not merely historical figures but are divinely appointed. This underscores God's sovereignty in orchestrating history and salvation. In the Christian faith, recognizing that Jesus' lineage includes Eliakim points to God's faithful raising up of the Messiah according to His purpose. The name thus invites believers to trust in God's power to establish and uphold His promises.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 1:13 states, "And Zorobabel begat Abiud; and Abiud begat Eliakim; and Eliakim begat Azor;" situating Eliakim within the direct genealogy of Jesus. The presence of Eliakim here highlights God's providential raising up of the Messiah's ancestors, reinforcing the divine hand in the unfolding of salvation history. The name Eliakim in this verse serves as a reminder that each link in the lineage is part of God's sovereign plan to establish His kingdom through Christ.
